pages.title: REGRESSION METRICS CHEAT SHEET
pages.subtitle: How far off are your numbers, really?
pages.learner: Is a lower RMSE always better?

panels.heading: Residuals: The Raw Material
panels.body:
Residual e = y - y_hat (true minus predicted).
Every regression metric summarizes the residuals.
panels.diagram: Scatter of points around a fitted line; short vertical segments from each point to the line labeled e, cyan above the line (e > 0), violet below (e < 0).

panels.heading: MAE, MSE, RMSE
panels.body:
MAE (mean absolute error) = mean(|e|): typical miss, target units.
MSE (mean squared error) = mean(e^2): punishes big misses.
RMSE = sqrt(MSE): back in target units.
RMSE >= MAE; a big gap = a few large errors.
panels.diagram: Three small bars side by side for the same residuals: MAE short, RMSE taller, with a bracket labeled 'gap = large errors'. Tiny |e| (V shape) and e^2 (parabola) icons above MAE and MSE.

panels.heading: R-Squared and Adjusted R-Squared
panels.body:
R^2 = 1 - SS_res / SS_tot: share of variance explained.
1 = perfect, 0 = no better than predicting the mean, < 0 = worse.
Adjusted R^2 = 1 - (1 - R^2)(n - 1)/(n - p - 1) penalizes extra features.
panels.diagram: Two panels of the same points: left with a flat dashed line at mean(y) and long gray gaps labeled SS_tot; right with the fitted line and short amber gaps labeled SS_res. A gauge from below 0 to 1 labeled 'worse than mean / mean / perfect'.

panels.heading: Worked Example
panels.diagram: A four-row table with columns y, y_hat, e, |e|, e^2 and a totals row (6 and 14). Highlight the e = 3 row in amber with a note 'one miss = 9 of 14 squared error'.

panels.heading: MAPE Pitfalls
panels.body:
MAPE (mean absolute percentage error) = mean(|e| / |y|) x 100%.
Explodes near y = 0; undefined at y = 0.
Asymmetric: under-forecasts cap at 100%, over-forecasts are unbounded.
Safer: WAPE = sum|e| / sum|y|.
panels.diagram: Curve of percentage error vs true value y for a fixed miss of 1 unit, shooting upward as y approaches 0, with an orange warning sign 'divide by ~0'.

panels.heading: Read the Residual Plot
panels.body:
Plot residuals vs predictions.
Random cloud around 0 = healthy.
Funnel = variance grows with y (try a log target).
Curve = missed nonlinearity.
A few far points = outliers dominating MSE.
panels.diagram: Three mini residual plots in a row with a horizontal zero line: a lime 'healthy' random cloud, an amber funnel widening to the right, and a violet U-shaped curve.

panels.heading: Choosing a Metric
panels.body:
Big misses are costly -> RMSE.
Outliers are noise; want the typical miss -> MAE.
Unit-free comparison -> R^2, used with care.
Relative error, y far from 0 -> MAPE or WAPE.
Always show a predict-the-mean baseline.
panels.diagram: A decision flow: 'Are big misses extra costly?' yes -> RMSE, no -> 'Need relative error?' yes -> WAPE/MAPE, no -> MAE. A small baseline bar labeled 'predict mean(y)' beside the results.

panels.heading: Pitfalls and Check Yourself
panels.body:
Training R^2 never drops when you add features.
RMSE depends on scale: never compare it across targets.
Q: errors [1, 1, 1, 9]. MAE or RMSE larger?
A: RMSE = 4.6 vs MAE = 3.0.
panels.diagram: Orange warning icons next to the first two lines; a quiz card with the question and the answer on a flip tab.

pages.footer: Look at the residuals first, then pick the number that matches the cost of a miss.
pages.summary: How to measure regression error: MAE, MSE, RMSE and R-squared, why MAPE misbehaves near zero, how to read residual plots, and how to choose the metric that matches the real cost of a miss.

pages.title: RANKING & RETRIEVAL METRICS
pages.subtitle: Did the right items land at the top?
pages.learner: Recall@10 looks fine. Why are users unhappy?

panels.heading: The Setup
panels.body:
A query returns a ranked list.
Each item is relevant (1) or not (0), or graded (0-3).
k = how many top results you score.
Metrics differ in how much position matters.
panels.diagram: A search box with a query feeding a vertical ranked list of five result cards numbered 1-5, relevant ones marked with a lime check, others gray. A bracket over the top 3 labeled 'k = 3'.

panels.heading: Precision@k, Recall@k, Hit Rate
panels.body:
Precision@k = relevant in top k / k.
Recall@k = relevant in top k / all relevant.
Hit rate@k = 1 if any relevant item is in the top k.
All three ignore order inside the top k.
panels.diagram: The same top-k bracket with two fractions drawn as bars: 'found / k' (precision) and 'found / all relevant' (recall), plus a single lamp icon lit for hit rate.

panels.heading: MRR and MAP
panels.body:
MRR (mean reciprocal rank) = mean of 1 / rank of the first relevant item.
AP (average precision) = mean of precision@i at each relevant rank i.
MAP = mean AP over all queries.
panels.diagram: Three queries as short rows; first relevant item at rank 1, 2 and 4 with labels 1, 1/2, 1/4 and their average MRR = 0.58.

panels.heading: NDCG: Graded and Position-Aware
panels.body:
NDCG = normalized discounted cumulative gain.
DCG@k = sum of rel_i / log2(i + 1) for i = 1..k.
NDCG = DCG / IDCG, the DCG of the ideal order; range 0 to 1.
Lower ranks count less.
panels.diagram: A descending staircase of discount weights by rank: 1.00, 0.63, 0.50, 0.43, 0.39. Beside it, the actual list and the ideal sorted list stacked to compare.

panels.heading: Worked Example
panels.diagram: Five numbered result cards with relevance 0,1,1,0,1, each card annotated with its discount (1/log2(i+1)) and its precision@i where relevant. Totals boxed at the bottom.

panels.heading: Offline vs Online
panels.body:
Offline: labeled queries; fast and repeatable, but labels miss new items.
Online: clicks, dwell time, conversions in an A/B test; real but noisy and position-biased.
Confirm offline wins online.
panels.diagram: Split panel: left a lab bench with a labeled query set and a scoreboard; right live users clicking results with a heatmap fading down the list. Arrow 'ship candidates' from left to right.

panels.heading: Evaluating RAG Retrieval
panels.body:
RAG = retrieval-augmented generation.
Retriever: recall@k of gold passages (did the evidence reach the context?).
Then MRR or NDCG for ordering.
Grade answer faithfulness separately.
panels.diagram: Pipeline: question -> retriever -> top-5 chunks -> LLM -> answer. A cyan probe on the chunks labeled 'recall@5, MRR' and a violet probe on the answer labeled 'faithful to chunks?'.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Unjudged items counted as irrelevant underrate new systems.
Averages hide failures on rare queries; inspect per query.
Precision@k is capped when fewer than k items are relevant.
Always state k.
panels.diagram: Orange warning tags: a result card with a '?' label (unjudged), a bar chart where one tiny query bar is red, and a sticky note 'k = ?'.

pages.footer: Hits get you into the list; rank decides whether anyone sees them.
pages.summary: How to score ranked results: precision@k, recall@k, hit rate, MRR, MAP and NDCG with one worked list, the gap between offline labels and online behavior, and how to evaluate the retrieval step of a RAG system.

pages.title: CALIBRATION CHEAT SHEET
pages.subtitle: When the model says 80%, is it right 80%?
pages.learner: My model is accurate. Why recalibrate?

panels.heading: What Calibration Means
panels.body:
Calibrated: among predictions made with confidence p, a fraction p are correct.
Of 100 cases scored 0.8, about 80 should be positive.
Matters when scores drive decisions, costs or abstention.
panels.diagram: A weather-forecast style card '80% chance' over a grid of 100 small squares, 80 lime and 20 gray.

panels.heading: Reliability Diagram
panels.body:
Bin predictions by confidence (e.g. 10 bins).
Plot mean confidence (x) vs observed accuracy (y).
On the diagonal = calibrated.
Below it = overconfident. Above it = underconfident.
panels.diagram: Square plot 0-1 on both axes with a dashed diagonal; cyan bars per bin sitting below the diagonal at high confidence, with orange gap shading labeled 'overconfident'. A histogram strip underneath shows bin counts.

panels.heading: ECE: Expected Calibration Error
panels.body:
ECE = sum over bins of (n_b / N) x |acc_b - conf_b|.
Weighted average gap between confidence and accuracy.
0 = perfect. Value depends on the binning, so report it.
panels.diagram: The reliability bars with each gap drawn as a vertical amber segment, segments weighted by bin size and summed into one ECE gauge.

panels.heading: Worked Example
panels.body:
100 predictions, 2 bins:
Bin A: 60 items, conf 0.90, acc 0.75 -> gap 0.15
Bin B: 40 items, conf 0.60, acc 0.55 -> gap 0.05
ECE = 0.6 x 0.15 + 0.4 x 0.05 = 0.11 (overconfident)
panels.diagram: Two-row table with columns items, conf, acc, gap, weight; the two weighted terms 0.09 and 0.02 adding to 0.11 in a boxed result.

panels.heading: Brier Score and Log Loss
panels.body:
Brier = mean (p - y)^2; 0 is best, always saying 0.5 scores 0.25.
Log loss = -mean[y log p + (1 - y) log(1 - p)]; one 0.99-confident miss costs 4.6.
Both reward calibration and sharpness.
panels.diagram: Two penalty curves vs predicted p for a true positive: Brier a gentle parabola, log loss shooting to infinity as p -> 0, with a red dot at p = 0.01 labeled 4.6.

panels.heading: Fixing It After Training
panels.body:
Fit on a held-out calibration set, never on training data.
Platt scaling: logistic fit on the score (2 parameters).
Isotonic regression: monotone steps; flexible, needs ~1,000+ points.
Temperature scaling: logits / T; argmax unchanged.
panels.code: probs = torch.softmax(logits / T, dim=-1)  # T > 1 softens
panels.diagram: Three small mapping curves from raw score to calibrated probability: a smooth S (Platt), a staircase (isotonic), and a family of softmax curves flattening as T grows (temperature).

panels.heading: Calibration vs Discrimination
panels.body:
Discrimination: are positives ranked above negatives? (AUROC)
Calibration: are the probabilities honest? (ECE)
A model can hit AUROC 0.95 and still be badly calibrated.
Platt scaling a binary score leaves AUROC unchanged.
panels.diagram: 2x2 grid: rows good/bad ranking, columns good/bad calibration, each cell with a tiny reliability plot and ROC curve; the 'good ranking, bad calibration' cell highlighted.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Calibration breaks under distribution shift; re-check on new data.
Deep nets and RLHF-tuned LLMs often run overconfident.
Check per-class reliability, not only the average.
Few points per bin = noisy ECE.
panels.diagram: Orange warning icons: a reliability curve that bends away on a 'new data' tab, and a nearly empty bin with a question mark.

pages.footer: Accuracy says how often you are right; calibration says when to believe you.
pages.summary: What it means for predicted probabilities to be calibrated, how to measure it with reliability diagrams, ECE, Brier score and log loss, how to fix it with Platt, isotonic or temperature scaling, and why calibration is different from ranking quality.

pages.title: A/B TESTING CHEAT SHEET
pages.subtitle: Is the difference real, or just noise?

panels.heading: Hypothesis Testing
panels.body:
H0 (null): A and B perform the same.
H1: they differ.
Ask how surprising the data would be if H0 were true.
alpha = 0.05 = the false-positive rate you accept.
panels.diagram: Bell curve of the test statistic under H0 with both 2.5% tails shaded orange as the rejection region; an arrow marks the observed value landing in a tail.

panels.heading: p-Values: What They Mean
panels.body:
p = P(data at least this extreme | H0 true).
NOT the probability that H0 is true.
NOT the size or importance of the effect.
p > 0.05 is not proof of no effect.
panels.diagram: One lime check card with the correct definition and three orange crossed-out cards with the common misreadings.

panels.heading: Confidence Intervals
panels.body:
95% CI: built so that 95% of such intervals cover the true effect.
Shows effect size and uncertainty together.
If the CI for the difference excludes 0, p < 0.05.
Report the CI, not just p.
panels.diagram: A number line centered on 0 with three horizontal interval bars: one wide crossing 0 (inconclusive), one narrow clearly right of 0 (real lift), one tiny near 0 (real but negligible).

panels.heading: Power and Sample Size
panels.body:
Power = P(detecting a real effect); aim for 80%.
Inputs: alpha, baseline rate p, minimum detectable effect (MDE).
Rule of thumb per arm: n ~ 16 p(1 - p) / MDE^2 (alpha 0.05, power 80%).
panels.diagram: Two overlapping bell curves (H0 and H1) with alpha shaded orange and power shaded lime; a slider below labeled 'more samples -> narrower curves -> more power'.

panels.heading: Worked Example
panels.diagram: Two conversion bars A and B with counts, and below them an interval bar from 0.4 to 1.8 points clearly to the right of a zero line.

panels.heading: Multiple Testing
panels.body:
20 metrics at alpha 0.05 -> about 1 false win by chance.
Bonferroni: test each at alpha / m (strict).
Benjamini-Hochberg: controls the false discovery rate (FDR); more power.
Pre-register one primary metric.
panels.diagram: A grid of 20 dice-like metric tiles, one lit up in amber labeled 'lucky p = 0.03'; beside it a threshold line dropping from 0.05 to 0.0025 labeled 'Bonferroni, m = 20'.

panels.heading: Comparing Two Models Fairly
panels.body:
Same test set, same preprocessing, several random seeds.
Use paired tests: McNemar, or a paired bootstrap.
Bootstrap: resample examples with replacement ~1,000x, recompute the metric, take the 2.5th-97.5th percentiles.
panels.diagram: Two model icons scoring the same stack of examples; a fan of resampled stacks feeding a histogram of metric differences with the middle 95% bracketed.

panels.heading: Pitfalls: Peeking
panels.body:
Checking daily and stopping at the first p < 0.05: false positives rise to ~19% with 10 looks.
Fix the sample size in advance, or use a sequential test.
Also watch novelty effects and uneven splits.
panels.diagram: A jagged p-value line over days dipping briefly below a dashed 0.05 line, with an orange 'STOP HERE?' flag at the dip and a calendar marking the planned end date.

pages.footer: Fix the plan and sample size first, then report effect sizes with intervals.
pages.summary: How to tell a real improvement from noise: hypothesis tests, what p-values do and do not mean, confidence intervals, power and sample size with a worked example, multiple-testing corrections, the bootstrap, the peeking problem and fair model comparisons.

pages.title: REGRESSION LOSSES CHEAT SHEET
pages.subtitle: What you minimize decides what you predict
pages.learner: Why did one outlier wreck my fit?

panels.heading: Loss vs Metric
panels.body:
Loss: what the optimizer minimizes in training; needs useful gradients.
Metric: what you report to people; can be anything.
They may differ: train on MSE, report MAE.
panels.diagram: Two gauges: an engine-room dial 'loss (optimizer sees)' wired to the training loop, and a dashboard dial 'metric (humans see)'.

panels.heading: MSE: The Gaussian View
panels.body:
L = (y - y_hat)^2, with residual e = y - y_hat.
Minimizer: the conditional MEAN.
Same as maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise.
Gradient 2e grows with the error, so big residuals dominate.
panels.diagram: A bell curve of noise around the true line, and a parabola loss curve below it labeled 'gradient grows with e'.

panels.heading: MAE: The Median
panels.body:
L = |y - y_hat|.
Minimizer: the conditional MEDIAN; robust to outliers.
Maximum likelihood under Laplace noise.
Gradient is always +/-1 and undefined at 0: slow, jittery near the optimum.
panels.diagram: A sharp-peaked Laplace noise curve, and a V-shaped loss curve below with constant-slope arrows on both sides.

panels.heading: Huber Loss
panels.body:
L = 0.5 e^2 if |e| <= delta, else delta(|e| - 0.5 delta).
Smooth near 0 like MSE, linear in the tails like MAE.
delta sets where errors count as outliers.
panels.diagram: Loss vs residual plot: a parabola in the middle joining straight lines at +/-delta, with the switch points marked by amber dots.

panels.heading: Quantile (Pinball) Loss
panels.body:
L = q*e if e >= 0, else (q - 1)*e.
q = 0.5 -> half of MAE (the median).
q = 0.9 -> under-predicting costs 9x more, so the model learns the 90th percentile.
Train q = 0.1 and 0.9 for an 80% interval.
panels.diagram: A tilted V loss curve (steep on the under-prediction side, shallow on the other); beside it a forecast line with a shaded band between the 0.1 and 0.9 quantile lines.

panels.heading: Worked Example: One Outlier
panels.body:
Targets y = [1, 2, 3, 4, 100]. Best constant prediction:
MSE -> mean = 22 (dragged up by 100)
MAE -> median = 3
Huber (delta = 1) -> 3: the outlier's pull is capped.
panels.diagram: Number line with five dots, the 100 far right in orange; three markers placed at 22 (MSE, pulled right), 3 (MAE) and 3 (Huber), with a rope from 100 tugging the MSE marker.

panels.heading: Outlier Behavior and Choosing
panels.body:
At e = 10: squared 100, Huber(1) 9.5, absolute 10.
Gaussian noise, want the mean -> MSE.
Heavy tails or bad labels -> Huber or MAE.
Asymmetric costs or intervals -> quantile loss.
panels.diagram: Overlay plot of loss vs residual from -4 to 4: MSE parabola (cyan), MAE V (lime), Huber (violet) and pinball q = 0.9 (amber), labeled where each curve sits at large |e|.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Scale targets first: MSE on raw dollars gives huge gradients.
Huber's delta is in target units; retune after rescaling.
Model trained on a log target predicts roughly the median, not the mean.
panels.diagram: Orange warning icons: an exploding gradient arrow over a '$' axis, a ruler showing delta shrinking after rescaling, and a skewed distribution with mean and median marked apart.

pages.footer: Choose the loss for the statistic you want: mean, median or quantile.
pages.summary: How regression losses differ from metrics, why MSE predicts the mean and MAE the median, how Huber and quantile losses handle outliers and asymmetric costs, and how to pick a loss for your noise and goals.

pages.title: CLASSIFICATION LOSSES CHEAT SHEET
pages.subtitle: Scores to probabilities, then punish confident mistakes

panels.heading: Softmax and Cross-Entropy
panels.body:
Softmax: p_i = exp(z_i) / sum_j exp(z_j), from logits z.
Cross-entropy: L = -log p_true.
Gradient on logits = p - one_hot(y).
Accuracy has no useful gradient, so we train on this smooth proxy.
panels.diagram: Pipeline: logits bar chart -> softmax box -> probability bar chart summing to 1 -> '-log' box -> loss value, with the true class bar outlined in lime.

panels.heading: Worked Example
panels.body:
Logits z = [2.0, 1.0, 0.1], true class 0.
Softmax p = [0.66, 0.24, 0.10]
L = -ln 0.66 = 0.42
If class 2 were true: L = -ln 0.10 = 2.32
Gradient = [-0.34, 0.24, 0.10]
panels.diagram: Three-column table (class, logit, p) with the true class highlighted; a small arrow showing gradient descent raising z_0 and lowering z_1, z_2.

panels.heading: Binary Cross-Entropy With Logits
panels.body:
BCE = -[y log s(z) + (1 - y) log(1 - s(z))], s = sigmoid.
Sigmoid then log fails: s(-800) = 0 -> log 0 = -inf.
Stable form: max(z, 0) - z*y + log(1 + exp(-|z|)).
panels.diagram: Two paths from a logit: an orange path 'sigmoid -> log' ending in a NaN skull icon, and a lime path 'fused stable formula' ending in a clean number.

panels.heading: Hinge Loss
panels.body:
Labels y in {-1, +1}, score f(x).
L = max(0, 1 - y f(x)).
Zero once the margin y f(x) >= 1: easy examples stop contributing.
Used by SVMs (support vector machines); gives no probabilities.
panels.diagram: Loss vs margin y*f(x): a straight line falling to 0 at margin 1 then flat; overlaid dashed log-loss curve that never quite reaches 0.

panels.heading: Focal Loss
panels.body:
FL = -(1 - p_t)^gamma log p_t, usually gamma = 2.
p_t = probability of the true class.
At p_t = 0.9 the loss shrinks 100x vs cross-entropy.
Focuses training on hard examples among many easy negatives.
panels.diagram: Loss vs p_t curves for gamma = 0, 1, 2, 5, with the easy region p_t > 0.6 shaded and labeled 'down-weighted'.

panels.heading: Label Smoothing and Class Weights
panels.body:
Label smoothing: target = (1 - eps) one-hot + eps / K, e.g. eps = 0.1. Stops logits growing without bound.
Class weights: scale each class's loss, e.g. by inverse frequency, so rare classes count.
panels.diagram: A hard target bar chart [1, 0, 0] morphing into a soft one [0.93, 0.03, 0.03] for K = 3; beside it a scale where one rare-class weight balances many common examples.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
CrossEntropyLoss expects raw logits; adding softmax first double-squashes.
Log of a probability that hit 0 -> NaN.
Class weights and focal loss distort probabilities; recalibrate before using them as odds.
panels.diagram: Orange warning icons: a softmax box drawn twice in a row crossed out, and a probability bar labeled 'not calibrated after reweighting'.

panels.heading: Check Yourself
panels.body:
p_true = 0.5 -> L = 0.69.
p_true = 0.01 -> L = ?
Answer: -ln 0.01 = 4.6, as costly as about 7 coin-flip guesses.
panels.diagram: Quiz card with a log-loss curve, two dots at p = 0.5 and p = 0.01, the answer hidden under a flip tab.

pages.footer: Feed raw logits to a fused loss and let cross-entropy punish confident mistakes.
pages.summary: How classifiers are trained: softmax with cross-entropy and its gradient, numerically stable binary cross-entropy on logits, hinge and focal losses, label smoothing and class weights, with a worked numeric example and common bugs.

pages.title: CONTRASTIVE & RANKING LOSSES
pages.subtitle: Pull matches together, push mismatches apart
pages.learner: Where do the negatives come from?

panels.heading: The Idea
panels.body:
Learn an embedding space: similar items close, different items far.
Anchor + positive (a match) + negatives (non-matches).
Similarity: cosine, or distance on normalized vectors.
panels.diagram: A 2D embedding map: an anchor dot (cyan), a positive (lime) with an inward arrow, and several negatives (orange) with outward arrows.

panels.heading: Contrastive Pair Loss
panels.body:
Pair distance d, label y (1 = similar):
L = y d^2 + (1 - y) max(0, m - d)^2.
Similar pairs are pulled to 0.
Dissimilar pairs are pushed past margin m, then ignored.
panels.diagram: Two pairs: a similar pair connected by a spring pulling together; a dissimilar pair with a dashed circle of radius m around one point and the other pushed outside it.

panels.heading: Triplet Loss
panels.body:
L = max(0, d(a, p) - d(a, n) + m).
The negative must be at least m farther than the positive.
Example: d(a, p) = 0.4, d(a, n) = 0.6, m = 0.5 -> L = 0.3.
panels.diagram: Anchor a at center, positive p at radius 0.4, negative n at radius 0.6, and a margin ring at 0.9 showing n still inside the danger zone.

panels.heading: InfoNCE / NT-Xent
panels.body:
Softmax over 1 positive and N - 1 negatives:
L = -log( exp(s_pos / tau) / sum_j exp(s_j / tau) ).
In-batch negatives: other batch items are free negatives.
Low temperature tau (e.g. 0.07) focuses on hard negatives.
panels.diagram: A row of similarity scores for one anchor, the positive in lime, fed through a softmax bar chart; a tau dial showing the bars sharpening as tau drops.

panels.heading: Worked Example: CLIP
panels.body:
CLIP: contrastive language-image pretraining.
Batch of N image-text pairs -> N x N similarity matrix.
Diagonal = true pairs; each row has N - 1 negatives.
Loss = cross-entropy over rows and columns, averaged.
panels.code:
logits = img @ txt.T / tau  # both L2-normalized
labels = torch.arange(len(img))
loss = (F.cross_entropy(logits, labels)
        + F.cross_entropy(logits.T, labels)) / 2
panels.diagram: A 4x4 grid with image thumbnails down the side and captions across the top; diagonal cells glowing lime, off-diagonal cells dim orange.

panels.heading: Hard Negative Mining
panels.body:
Random negatives get too easy: loss -> 0, no signal.
Hard negatives: close to the anchor but wrong, e.g. top keyword-search hits that are not the answer.
Too hard = likely false negatives.
panels.diagram: Concentric rings around the anchor labeled easy (far), semi-hard (inside margin), hard (closer than the positive); one 'hard' point tagged with an orange '?' as a possible unlabeled match.

panels.heading: Pairwise Ranking: BPR and RankNet
panels.body:
Score item i above item j for the same user or query.
BPR (Bayesian personalized ranking): L = -log sigmoid(s_i - s_j).
RankNet: logistic loss on score differences.
Only the order matters.
panels.diagram: Two item cards for one user: 'clicked' i and 'not clicked' j with scores; a sigmoid curve of s_i - s_j showing loss falling as the gap grows.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Small batches = few negatives = weak InfoNCE signal.
Duplicates in a batch become false negatives.
tau too low -> unstable; too high -> blurry embeddings.
No negatives -> collapse to one point.
panels.diagram: Orange warning icons: a tiny batch tray, two identical images marked 'negative?', and an embedding map where all dots have collapsed to one spot.

pages.footer: Make the right match win a softmax over the wrong ones.
pages.summary: How embedding models learn by comparison: contrastive pair and triplet losses with margins, InfoNCE with temperature and in-batch negatives, the CLIP loss, hard negative mining, and pairwise ranking losses like BPR and RankNet.

pages.title: GENERATIVE MODEL LOSSES
pages.subtitle: Most losses are a log-likelihood in disguise
pages.learner: How does a GAN even have a loss?

panels.heading: Maximum Likelihood
panels.body:
Pick parameters theta that make the observed data most probable.
Minimize NLL (negative log-likelihood) = -sum log p_theta(x_i).
Gaussian noise -> MSE. Categorical -> cross-entropy.
panels.diagram: A histogram of data with two candidate density curves; the better-fitting curve glows cyan with a higher 'likelihood' meter.

panels.heading: Next-Token Loss and Perplexity
panels.body:
LLMs minimize mean -log p(x_t | x_<t) over tokens.
Perplexity = exp(mean NLL): effective number of choices.
Example: loss 2.0 nats -> perplexity e^2 = 7.4.
panels.diagram: A sentence 'the cat sat on the' with a next-token probability bar chart over candidate words; 'mat' highlighted with p = 0.4 and -log p = 0.92 shown.

panels.heading: KL Divergence
panels.body:
KL(P || Q) = sum P log(P / Q) >= 0; 0 only if P = Q.
Asymmetric: P = [0.5, 0.5], Q = [0.9, 0.1] -> KL(P||Q) = 0.51, KL(Q||P) = 0.37.
Fitting Q: forward KL covers modes, reverse KL picks one.
panels.diagram: A two-humped target P (violet); a wide Q covering both humps labeled 'forward KL' and a narrow Q sitting on one hump labeled 'reverse KL'.

panels.heading: ELBO for VAEs
panels.body:
VAE = variational autoencoder; ELBO = evidence lower bound on log p(x).
ELBO = E_q[log p(x|z)] - KL(q(z|x) || p(z)).
Reconstruction + a pull toward the prior N(0, I).
Train by maximizing it.
panels.diagram: Encoder -> latent z (Gaussian blob) -> decoder -> reconstruction; a lime arrow 'reconstruction term' between input and output, a violet arrow 'KL to N(0, I)' on the latent.

panels.heading: GAN Minimax
panels.body:
min_G max_D E[log D(x)] + E[log(1 - D(G(z)))].
Discriminator D learns real vs fake; generator G learns to fool it.
In practice G maximizes log D(G(z)) for stronger early gradients.
panels.diagram: Generator robot passing a fake image to a discriminator judge next to a stack of real images; a seesaw labeled min_G / max_D.

panels.heading: Diffusion: Predict the Noise
panels.body:
Noise the data: x_t = sqrt(a_bar_t) x_0 + sqrt(1 - a_bar_t) eps.
Train the network to recover eps with MSE.
A reweighted ELBO simplifies to this plain loss.
panels.code:
eps = torch.randn_like(x0)
xt = a_bar[t].sqrt() * x0 + (1 - a_bar[t]).sqrt() * eps
loss = F.mse_loss(model(xt, t), eps)
panels.diagram: A strip of one image going from clean to pure noise across timesteps t; at one step the network outputs a predicted noise patch compared to the true noise patch with an MSE arrow.

panels.heading: Compare at a Glance
panels.body:
Autoregressive LM: exact NLL.
VAE: lower bound (ELBO).
GAN: no likelihood; an adversarial game.
Diffusion: denoising MSE, a reweighted bound.
Likelihood losses are stable; adversarial ones are fragile.
panels.diagram: Four-row table with icons for each model family and columns 'loss', 'exact likelihood?', 'training stability'.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Perplexity across tokenizers is not comparable; use bits per byte.
VAE posterior collapse: decoder ignores z, KL -> 0.
GAN mode collapse: few distinct outputs.
Low NLL does not guarantee good samples.
panels.diagram: Orange warning icons: two rulers with different tick sizes, a latent blob disconnected from the decoder, and a generator outputting the same face repeatedly.

pages.footer: Know the likelihood behind your loss and you know what your model is learning.
pages.summary: The probabilistic view of training: maximum likelihood and negative log-likelihood, next-token loss and perplexity, KL divergence and its asymmetry, and the losses behind VAEs, GANs and diffusion models.
